newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices recover on good demand, tight supply.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices recover on good demand, tight supply.

text.p: World oil prices recovered on Friday, with dealers judging that low crude and heating fuel stocks coupled with healthy demand in industrialised economies still justified a bull market.
World benchmark Brent crude futures ended 41 cents higher in London at $24.00 a barrel.

Brent shed 69 cents on profit-taking on Thursday as speculators dumped long positions in gas oil futures, which had surged to five-year highs on supply worries ahead of the northern hemisphere winter.
Analysts believe that stocks of gas oil, a middle distillate used as heating fuel in Europe, are now low to cope with the possibility of a protracted, cold winter.

Household stocks in Germany, Europe's biggest heating oil market, are 5-10 percent below last year while in the United States, the world's biggest energy consumer, heating oil stocks are a third below year-ago levels.

Brokers Kleinwort Benson said strong global oil demand, low heating fuel inventories and rising political concerns about supply led it to raise its fourth quarter oil price forecast by $3.50 a barrel.
Crude prices are nearly $8 a barrel above 1995 levels but Kleinwort Benson said in its World Oil Report that prices were more likely to fall in early 1997 than rise.
"Oil prices may go even higher short-term but the market has for months been fed bullish news which must by now have largely been discounted," it said.
It said that in addition to healthy fundamentals, bullish speculators and hedgers were also partly responsible for higher prices in the short term.
Signs of some stock rebuilding resulted in a midweek selloff, though traders said there was a reluctance to sell the market short as the peak winter demand period had yet to hit.
But high heating oil prices could in the longer term encourage consumers to switch to cleaner and cheaper fuels, Kleinwort Benson said.
"Sustained high heating oil prices could induce conservation and substitution (in favour of natural gas), especially in the U.S.," it said.

Kleinwort expected oil production outside the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) to rise by nearly two million barrels per day (bpd) year in the first quarter of 1997, compared with the same period of 1996.

The 11 OPEC countries are producing slightly above their ceiling of 25.033 million bpd but the excess is being absorbed. The report said a rise in non-OPEC production would offset any further delay in Iraq's return to the oil market.
